name: Marbles
blurb: Small glass balls flicked with the thumb to knock out other players' marbles
title: Marbles: How the Game Was Played, History and Where It Stands
description: Marbles are small glass balls flicked with the thumb in playground games. An ancient pastime, mass-produced since 1903, still made and still played today.
h1: What is the game of marbles?
answer: Marbles are small balls, usually of glass and about 1 to 2 cm across, that children flick with the thumb to knock other players' marbles out of a ring, hit them, or roll them into holes in the ground. The pastime is ancient, and machine-made glass marbles from 1903 onward made them cheap enough for every child's pocket. Playground marble games are rarer than they were in the 1980s and 1990s, but marbles are still made in large numbers and a world championship is still held every year.

body: The classic glass marble is clear with a twist of coloured glass inside; others are solid colours or swirled opaque glass. Toy marbles range from about 0.5 to 3.5 cm, and most games use a slightly bigger marble, the shooter or taw, to hit the others. Many children kept one favourite shooter and never risked it.
Rules changed from street to street, but most games were variations on a few ideas:

ul: Ring taw: marbles go inside a circle drawn on the ground, and players shoot from outside to knock them out.
Holes: dig small holes in the dirt and get your marble into each one in turn.
Chase: two players take turns trying to hit each other's marble.
Knuckle down: the shooting hand keeps its knuckle on the ground while the thumb flicks the marble.

body: Playing "for keeps" (keepsies) meant you took home every marble you won, which is why a bulging pocket marked a good player. In China children played very similar games with glass marbles (弹珠, dànzhū), and in South Asia versions such as kanche and pili goli.

body: Very much. Vacor de Mexico is described as the world's largest maker of playing marbles, and Marble King in West Virginia is the last American toy-marble manufacturer. Marbles also live on in marble runs, Chinese checkers and as the glass stopper in Japanese Ramune soda bottles. Collectors pay attention to type, size and condition, and handmade art marbles are their own craft. What has faded is the everyday sight of children crouched over a ring in the dirt.

faq.q: What is a taw in marbles?
faq.a: The shooter: the marble, often a bit larger, that you flick to hit the others.

faq.q: What does playing for keeps mean?
faq.a: Playing so that the winner keeps the marbles they knock out, rather than handing them back after the game.

faq.q: Is there still a marbles championship?
faq.a: Yes. The British and World Marbles Championship has been held at Tinsley Green, West Sussex, every Good Friday since 1932.
